vignette:
He was twenty-six when the hurricane came-three years ago now, though it might as well be yesterday. The storm wasn't supposed to hit their town directly, but it shifted course overnight. By the time the warnings came, it was too late to leave. He remembers the sound most of all: a deep, unending roar, like a freight train running through the living room. Then the walls began to groan, and the roof lifted in sections, letting in the sky and the rain and the wind all at once. He and his mother huddled in the hallway closet, the only place left that felt solid. She held his hand so tightly he thought the bones would break. When the ceiling collapsed in the next room, the shock wave threw them against the far wall. He felt something crack in his shoulder, but he couldn't tell if it was his or hers.

They survived. His mother spent three weeks in the hospital with a punctured lung and a broken pelvis. He healed quickly-just a separated shoulder, some cuts. But the inside of him never healed the same way. Even now, when the wind picks up outside his apartment, he finds himself holding his breath, scanning the room for a place to hide. His sleep is broken by fragments of that night: the roar, the darkness, the smell of wet plaster. He wakes with his heart slamming against his ribs, convinced the ceiling is about to come down again.

He works as a salesperson at a car dealership, a job that used to come naturally. He was the guy who could chat up anyone, crack jokes, build rapport. Now, the open showroom floor feels exposed. The large windows make him edgy. When a customer mentions an upcoming storm on the news, his stomach tightens, and he has to excuse himself to the restroom to reset. His monthly numbers have slipped, not because he doesn't know the product, but because he struggles to sustain the easygoing energy customers expect. Twice this month, a manager pulled him aside to ask if everything was okay. He said yes, because there is no way to explain that the sound of a slamming car door makes him flinch and see the closet door buckling.

He avoids driving on rainy days. If he sees flood warnings on his phone, he takes a different route to work, even if it adds forty minutes. He canceled a date last week because the forecast showed a chance of thunderstorms. The woman was understanding, but he felt a familiar shame-the kind that tells him he is becoming someone smaller than he used to be. At night, he checks the weather app obsessively before turning off the light, sometimes three or four times. He keeps a flashlight and a bottle of water under the bed, just in case. He knows it's irrational. The house he grew up in was rebuilt. The odds of another hurricane hitting directly are low. But knowing doesn't stop the tightness from creeping into his chest when the barometer drops.

His social life has narrowed. He used to go out with friends from work, but now he makes excuses. Crowds feel unpredictable; loud noises make him jumpy. On the rare night he stays out late, he drinks too much to quiet the hypervigilance, and the next day he calls in sick with a headache. He has not spoken to his mother about it. She recovered, but she doesn't like to talk about the storm. They talk about everything else-weather, her garden, his job-never that night. He thinks maybe she has moved on. He wonders why he cannot.

A few weeks ago, he was driving home when he passed a construction site where a crew was tearing down a damaged building. The sound of the wrecking ball hitting concrete made his hands lock on the wheel. He had to pull over, heart racing, palms sweating, a wave of nausea rising. He sat there for fifteen minutes, telling himself it was just a job site, just a machine. But the feeling did not fully leave until he was inside his apartment with the door locked and the blinds drawn.

He has not told anyone the full story. Not his friends, not his coworkers, not the doctor he saw for his shoulder. He carries it alone, like a weight he cannot put down. Some days he wonders if the storm will ever really end for him, or if he will always be that person in the closet, waiting for the ceiling to fall.
